commentary.text:
**Move note.** Opening plan: the fastest realistic win here is the four-square center occupation, but neither side can just race — a single enemy piece parked in the middle denies it. So the real currency is captures: only three losses eliminate a color, and a sandwich requires the *mover* to be one flank, which means a stationary "anchor" next to the center is worth a lot. Any enemy piece that steps beside my anchor can be snapped up by bringing a second piece of the same color to the far side.

I'm sending Red from (0,4) straight down column 4 to (3,4). That claims one of the four central squares immediately and takes away Blue's easiest entry — Blue's row-3 run from (3,7) now stops at (3,5). Blue's natural way into the middle becomes row 4, and that is exactly where I want them: my intended follow-up is Yellow (7,3)→(4,3), after which an enemy piece on (4,4) can be sandwiched by Yellow (7,5)→(4,5), and an enemy piece on (3,3) can be sandwiched by Red (0,2)→(3,2). Two center squares held, two capture nets set over the remaining two.

Things I'm watching: Red on (3,4) is alone in enemy space, so I need to track Blue building a pair on (2,4)/(4,4) or (3,3)/(3,5) to sandwich it back, and I need columns 2 and 5 to stay open as my capture lanes — blocking those is the opponent's best quiet defense.
I’m taking a central square immediately, establishing a foothold for Team B while keeping the Blue piece clear of any current sandwich threat.

**Move note.** Blue answered by dropping (4,7)→(4,4), taking a central square directly beneath my Red. Two things follow from that. First, it creates a threat against me: Blue can play (2,7)→(2,4) and sandwich my Red on (3,4) between (2,4) and (4,4). That's Blue's move at ply 5, and since nothing of mine can reach (2,4) in one move, I plan to answer it on Red's turn at ply 4 — most likely by sliding (3,4)→(3,3), which sidesteps the sandwich while keeping a central square.

Second, Blue's piece on (4,4) is itself exposed, and that's what I take advantage of now. Yellow runs (7,3)→(4,3), claiming the second central square and planting an anchor immediately left of the Blue piece. The threat is Yellow (7,5)→(4,5): landing there looks left and sees Blue on (4,4) with my own Yellow on (4,3) beyond it — a clean sandwich, one loss for Blue out of the three that eliminate a color.

Verifying safety of the landing square: from (4,3) the four rays give nothing to either side — up, down and left are empty, and rightward the Blue piece is backed by an empty (4,5), so no capture fires for me and Blue's group still has breathing room. Yellow on (4,3) also can't be sandwiched soon, since Blue would need to reach (4,2), which is two moves away round the outside, and Green has no partner square on that file.

What I expect: the opponent's cheapest defense is plugging column 5 below row 4 — Green (5,0)→(5,5) or Blue (6,7)→(6,5) — to cut my Yellow's route to (4,5). If that happens I reroute via (7,6)→(4,6). My team now sits on two of the four central squares.
I’m advancing Green to (5,5), where it blocks Yellow’s direct route to (4,5). That prevents an immediate Yellow sandwich of the central Blue piece and lets Team B retain its foothold.

**Move note.** Green's (5,0)→(5,5) was exactly the expected defense: it plugs column 5 so my Yellow on (7,5) can no longer run up to (4,5) and sandwich the Blue piece on (4,4). Meanwhile Blue has a real threat of its own — (2,7)→(2,4) would trap my Red on (3,4) between (2,4) and Blue's (4,4). Nothing I own can reach (2,4) in one move, so the piece has to step aside.

I'm sliding it just one square: (3,4)→(3,3). This dodges the sandwich without conceding anything, because (3,3) is also one of the four central squares — my team still holds two of them, now (3,3) and (4,3), stacked as a solid pair. Checking the landing: downward from (3,3) I see my own Yellow on (4,3) backed by an empty (5,3), so no friendly-fire capture fires; the other three rays are empty. And neither Blue nor Green has a one-move sandwich against me — Blue's only pattern is landing on (4,2) to squeeze my Yellow against (4,4), and Blue has no piece that can get to (4,2) in a single move.

The point of retreating to (3,3) rather than to (3,5) is the trap it leaves behind. Blue's natural move is now (3,7)→(3,4), grabbing the square I just vacated. If Blue does that, Red (0,5)→(3,5) runs straight down the open column 5 and lands beside it, with my Red on (3,3) waiting on the far side — Blue's piece is captured.

Longer-term caution I'm noting for myself: Red on (3,3) above Yellow on (4,3) is a two-piece line in an open file, and Green could eventually pincer it by taking both (2,3) and (5,3), which would capture both at once. I must not add more pieces to that column — that only lengthens the line the pincer would sweep. The right answer will be denying Green access to those squares.
I’m shifting Blue to (3,4), taking the open upper-center square and forming a useful Blue flank beside the central Red piece. Green is positioned to obstruct Red’s most direct sandwich response.

**Move note.** Blue's (4,4)→(3,4) was a mistake in my view: it vacated a central square to attack, and now the middle is (3,3) Red, (4,3) Yellow, (3,4) Blue, and (4,4) **empty**. I'm taking it — Yellow (7,4)→(4,4), straight up the open column 4.

That gives my team three of the four central squares. The whole game now hinges on (3,4), and I already have the tool for it: Red (0,5)→(3,5) runs down the empty column 5 and lands beside Blue's piece with my Red on (3,3) waiting beyond it — a sandwich that removes Blue from (3,4) entirely. After that capture my Red would sit on (3,5), which also seals row 3 against Blue's remaining pieces on column 7, and a later (3,5)→(3,4) completes all four central squares for the win.

The new Yellow pair on (4,3)–(4,4) is more than a land grab; it poisons the squares Green would want. If Green drops onto (4,5), Yellow (7,6)→(4,6) sandwiches it against my (4,4). If Green drops onto (4,2), Yellow (7,1)→(4,1) sandwiches it against my (4,3). Both escape lanes up columns 1 and 6 are currently clear, so Green's natural pincer against my row-4 pair costs Green a piece on the first step.

Checking my landing square: from (4,4) the ray upward hits Blue on (3,4) backed by an empty (2,4), so nothing fires; left is my own Yellow; down and right are empty. And Green has no capture anywhere on the board next turn — every line I can find runs into an empty square before reaching a second Green.

What I expect is Green plugging column 5 at (1,5) or (2,5) to save Blue's piece. The threat I'm watching against me is Blue working a piece round to (5,4) via row 6, which would squeeze my new Yellow against Blue's (3,4) — but that takes two moves, and my Red capture should remove the anchor first.
I’m moving Green to (2,5) to block the Red piece on (0,5) from reaching (3,5), which protects Blue on (3,4) from the immediate horizontal sandwich.

**Move note.** Green's (5,5)→(2,5) plugged column 5 above, so my planned Red (0,5)→(3,5) sandwich on Blue's (3,4) is off the table for now. But Green vacating row 5 opened something far more urgent: **row 5 is completely empty**, and Blue (5,7)→(5,4) would land under my Yellow on (4,4) and sandwich it against Blue's own piece on (3,4). That costs me a piece and, worse, tears a hole in the three central squares I currently hold.

Nothing of mine can occupy (5,4) — column 4 is corked by Blue on (3,4) and my own Yellow on (4,4) — so I block the lane instead. Red (0,6) runs the length of the empty column 6 down to (5,6), standing directly in front of Blue's (5,7) and cutting the only path to (5,4). Row 5 from the left is barren of Blue pieces and column 4 from below has none either, so this single block kills the threat outright.

I checked the landing square: from (5,6) the rightward ray hits Blue on (5,7) and then the board edge, so nothing fires, and the other three rays are empty. Blue's counter would be reaching (5,5) to squeeze my new Red against (5,7), but row 5 rightward is now blocked by that very Red and there is no Blue anywhere on column 5, so it takes Blue two moves via (6,7)→(6,5)→(5,5) — I'll have warning.

Note that (3,6) was the tempting square instead, since it would let Red swing to (3,5) and sandwich Blue's (3,4) against my (3,3). I rejected it: Blue answers (3,4)→(3,5) and my Red on (3,6) is caught against Blue's (3,7).

The strategic picture is unchanged and still good for me — I hold three of the four central squares, and Blue's piece on (3,4) is the only thing between me and the win. It cannot leave that square, because I'm building toward being able to drop onto (3,4) the moment it does.
I’m staging Blue on (1,2), creating a direct threat to descend onto (3,2). With Blue already on (3,4), that would sandwich and capture the central Red piece on (3,3), forcing Red to respond.

**Move note.** Blue's (1,7)→(1,2) is a raid at my Red on (3,3): Blue wants (1,2)→(3,2), landing on the far side of my Red with Blue's own piece on (3,4) as the anchor, which would sweep Red off a central square. Column 2 is wide open, so that has to be answered.

Yellow (7,2)→(2,2) runs the whole length of that empty file and does three jobs at once. It corks column 2 so the (3,2) landing is unreachable — Blue's only other route into row 3's left side is the three-move detour (1,2)→(1,1)→(3,1)→(3,2). It boxes in the Blue raider, which now has (0,2) Red above and my Yellow below and can only shuffle sideways. And most importantly it lands on the launch square for my main plan.

That plan is the point of the move. From (2,2), Yellow slides along the empty row 2 to (2,4) — and landing there looks straight down at Blue on (3,4) with my own Yellow on (4,4) beyond it. Blue's last central square gets captured. Then Yellow (2,4)→(3,4) fills the hole and my team holds (3,3), (3,4), (4,3), (4,4) — all four, and the game.

Landing checks: upward from (2,2) the ray runs Blue (1,2), Red (0,2), then the board edge — no Yellow at the end, so nothing fires and my own Red is not caught in friendly fire. The other three rays are empty. Blue's raider still has (1,1) free so no enclosure. And Green has no capture anywhere next turn — I walked every Green line and each one hits an empty square before finding a second Green.

Things to arrange with my Red turns: once Blue's piece is gone from (3,4), the only enemy path back to it is Blue (3,7) sliding along row 3, so I want a Red parked on (3,5) or otherwise sealing that lane before the capture lands.

I’m tightening a Green clamp around Yellow’s blocker on (2,2) while keeping Green on (2,5) in place to protect the central Blue piece. If Yellow remains, Green can move from (2,5) to (2,3) and capture it; if it retreats, Blue’s route toward the central Red reopens.

**Move note.** Green's (2,0)→(2,1) sets up (2,5)→(2,3), which would pin my Yellow on (2,2) between two Greens. I'm not defending that directly — Yellow moves before Green does, and it's leaving anyway.

The move I want is Red (0,5)→(0,4), loading the top of column 4. It looks quiet, but it's the key to the whole position: (1,4) and (2,4) are both empty, so this Red now stares straight down at Blue's piece on (3,4) — the one square standing between me and the four-square center win. If (3,4) ever empties, Red drops in and the game ends on the spot.

That combines with Yellow's plan into a double-decker. Next Yellow turn, (2,2)→(2,4) lands on Blue's head and captures it against my Yellow on (4,4). Then either Yellow itself steps down to (3,4) for the win, or — if Green grabs the Yellow by landing on (2,3) against its (2,5) partner — column 4 clears and Red (0,4)→(3,4) wins immediately instead. Green cannot block the file: (1,4) is unreachable for it with Blue sitting on (1,2), and (2,4) will be occupied by my Yellow.

Two constraints I'm respecting. First, my Red on (5,6) is pinned to duty: row 5 is otherwise empty, and Blue (5,7)→(5,4) would sandwich my Yellow on (4,4) against Blue's (3,4). That Red stays put until Blue's (3,4) piece dies, at which point the anchor is gone and the Red is free to swing up column 6 to (3,6) and seal Blue's last route back into (3,4) along row 3. Second, I will not put a second piece on row 2 next to my Yellow — Green landing on (2,4) would sweep the whole line back to its piece on (2,1).

No Blue capture exists next turn: row 5 is corked, column 2 is corked by my Yellow, and every other Blue ray runs into empty space.

I’m staging Blue on (6,4), threatening to move to (5,4) and sandwich Yellow on (4,4) against Blue on (3,4). Together with Green’s threat against Yellow on (2,2), this forces Yellow to choose which position to defend.

**Move note.** Blue's (6,7)→(6,4) was aimed at (5,4): landing there would trap my Yellow on (4,4) against Blue's own piece on (3,4). I'm answering that by removing the anchor and cashing in at the same time.

Yellow (2,2)→(2,4) slides along the empty row 2 and lands directly above Blue's central piece. Looking down from (2,4): Blue on (3,4), and beyond it my own Yellow on (4,4) — sandwich. Blue's piece is captured, its first loss of the three that would eliminate the color. That single move does four things: it takes a piece, it empties the last central square, it kills the (5,4) threat outright (with (3,4) empty, Blue landing on (5,4) sees only my Yellow and an empty square beyond, so nothing fires), and it puts my Yellow one step from the win.

The position after this is a fork Green cannot solve. My team holds (3,3), (4,3), (4,4), and (3,4) is empty with two of my pieces queued on column 4 — Yellow on (2,4) and Red behind it on (0,4). Yellow (2,4)→(3,4) simply wins. If Green instead takes my Yellow by landing on (2,3) against its partner on (2,5), that clears column 4 and Red (0,4)→(3,4) wins on the spot instead. Green cannot occupy (3,4) itself — row 3 from the left is corked by my Red on (3,3), the file is corked by my own pieces above and below, and coming round via (3,5) takes two moves.

That leaves exactly one defensive resource: Blue running (3,7) along row 3 into (3,4) on its next turn. So my Red turn is already spoken for — (5,6)→(3,6) up the empty column 6 seals that lane, and with Blue's (3,4) piece dead, the Red is no longer needed as a row-5 cork and can no longer be squeezed at (3,5), since Blue has nothing on column 5.
Yellow used the blocker to capture our central Blue, but in doing so stepped directly between the two Green pieces. I’m closing the clamp now and capturing Yellow on (2,4), keeping the exchange even.

**Move note.** Green took the bait. By landing on (2,3) to capture my Yellow on (2,4), Green cleared the very file it needed to keep blocked — and that was the losing half of the fork. Column 4 is now completely open: (1,4), (2,4) and (3,4) are all empty, with my Red waiting on (0,4).

Red (0,4)→(3,4) runs straight down and fills the last central square. My team then holds all four: Red on (3,3), Red on (3,4), Yellow on (4,3), Yellow on (4,4).

Checking the landing for any self-inflicted damage, since a capture that swept my own Yellow off (4,4) would undo the win: leftward the very first square is my own Red on (3,3), so no line forms; upward and rightward are empty; downward the ray runs Yellow (4,4) then the empty (5,4), so it terminates without reaching a Red and nothing is captured. My Yellows also can't be enclosed — (5,4), (5,3) and (4,2) are all open. Nothing is removed, and the four central squares stand occupied by Team A.

That's the center-occupation victory. Looking back, the game turned on treating the middle as a capture net rather than a footrace: the anchor on (3,3) plus the pair on (4,3)/(4,4) meant every square Blue tried to hold next to them was one move from being sandwiched, and stacking Yellow on (2,4) with Red behind it on (0,4) left the opponent with no answer that didn't open the file for the other piece.
